items.title: Linux in a Browser Tab
items.summary: Linux was once distributed on CDs and DVDs stuck to the front of computer magazines. Now, technology has advanced to the point where you can simply run a Linux kernel right in your browser. That’s precisely what you get with Unkernel from [pithings]. Unkernel is described as “Linux 7.x built as a single wasm module with an MMU.” Yes, thanks to the magic of WebAssembly, you can run Linux in a browser tab at a decent fraction of native speed. All the proper kernel stuff—like syscalls, the scheduler, memory management, file systems, and networking—is compiled code. User programs are then emulated with a just-in-time compiler, so you can run Ubuntu and Alpine packages without any fuss. You get a shell, package manager, persistent storage, sound, and internet access out of the box. It’s basically a whole Linux computer sitting in a single browser tab for your convenience. It’s generally not as fast as running the kernel natively, but where you need a little Linux on the go, it should come in clutch. We’ve discussed Linux showing up in weird places quite recently If you’re sticking kernels where they’re not expected, be sure to let us know on the tipsline. items.title: A Pen Plotter to Draw You Up (on) the Wall
items.summary: Back in our day you were told not to draw on the walls; nowadays we have robots for that– like Mural 2.0 by [Nik Ivanov]. If the name doesn’t give it away, this is a large format pen plotter made to draw, well, murals. It’s also not [Nik]’s first rodeo, though this version seems considerably improved from the orignial version. He’s now using a FluidNC board based on an ESP32 and TMC2209 stepper drivers, while the steppers they drive are a pair of NEMA 17 pancake units. Using pancakes for this application makes sense, as the steppers are on the machine and must pull themselves up against gravity using the single belt that is anchored at ceiling level. The kinematics of that mean you don’t get the full area between the anchor points– you lose 20% at the edges– but you can still get a pretty big mural going. In the demo/build video embedded below, it looks like you’re more limited by marker life, [Nik] cautioning that past about 500 m of line things can start to get a bit weak as the pen dries out. He’s working on a ‘pause and replace pen’ routine for the next firmware version to help with that project. For now, the WiFi-based interface [Nik] has on the ESP32 gives you that path length in advance, and can even process both SVG and raster images with both a sine-wave style squiggle and finite-curve style space filling. This isn’t the fastest pen plotter we’ve seen on these pages, and it might not quite be the simplest, either, but [Nik] has put together a very easy build that you could do with your nieces and nephews content in the knowledge that the easy-to-use firmware will let them keep making murals when you aren’t there– assuming, that is, that their mother lets them draw on the walls. items.title: Custom Firmware for Fortinet FortiGate 60 Firewall/Router
items.summary: When [Matt Williams] found an old enterprise firewall in the trash, he knew he had to do something with it. After cracking it open, he found that this 2000s-era Fortinet FortiGate 60 hardware firewall has some very hackable hardware in the form of a VIA C3 mainboard. This is an x86-compatible CPU that was very popular in small form-factor and industrial solutions around 2000s, meaning that it should be able to run just about anything that’s happy to run on its 400 MHz single core. Unfortunately it wasn’t a standard Mini-ITX C3 board like the one that [Matt] also has kicking around, as that one features standard DIMMs for the memory modules. For this firewall the 128 MB of SDRAM was soldered to the board, with the only clue as to how to initialize it in the original firmware. Ergo this firmware had to be reverse-engineered to figure out just how this was supposed to happen. With that done, Linux 2.4 was happy enough to boot on it with a bit more tweaking. Using the framebuffer driver applications like DOOM happily ran, as the above graphic shows. That it’s very much green is due to only the green pin on the VGA connector being probed. Since it’s a firewall Fortinet only added a physical DE-9 port in addition to the internal IDE interface and CF card slot. If one were to wire up these pads on the mainboard to physical connectors, it would actually make for a pretty decent little system for what the kids call retro gaming these days. With all that green, it almost looks like doom on an apple II! Even if I was young and didn’t use them much, those green and amber phosphor screens will always give me the warm fuzzies…at least a little bit, whenever I see them. They’re not only much smaller, they’re also less abrasive, and work with 0.2 mm nozzles. Although basically just found in industrial filaments right now, [JanTec Engineering] put a spool to the test to see what these whiskers bring to the party. While at an event in Japan, [JanTec] got handed a spool of Poticon STD1 NTL34M PA filament, presumably the common PA6, AKA Nylon. In their messaging the company calls it LEXTER, a bio-based polyamide. This was subsequently put to the test after returning home, with the recommended print settings and the newly constructed testing machine, called the Atlas 2000 . This is an open source testing machine that could be handy if you have about $500 lying around and an urgent need to test the tensile, compression and bending properties of materials. The filament under test is 20% TISMO by weight, with it scoring well in the tensile strength test, while being about as brittle as the datasheet suggests. Such reinforced polymers are generally known for being stiff and brittle, so this is little surprise. Perhaps the biggest advantage of this filament is that you can print finer details with it using an 0.2 mm nozzle, making it an interesting engineering filament in that respect. With a tracker the panel will instead follow the sun, potentially even adjusting the angle of the panel to optimize how much of the sun’s rays hit it during the day. The two-axis tracker that [Greenhill Forge] built is an example of how to make a tracker using just a steel frame and simple electronics . As noted in the video, commercial solar trackers tend to use slewing bearings , which support heavy, slow-turning structures like a PV panel array. These are however rather expensive, so instead he opted to use a trailer axle hub as the budget version. The array’s structure including a drive sprocket is built up on top of this axle in such a way that it easily removed for maintenance, mostly using welded steel to create a stable base for the PV panels. This also contains the second axis, with two bearings to pivot around. The azimuth axis is driven with a large geared electric motor, while the second axis is driven by a linear motor containing a worm gear. This should keep position very well, even in case of power loss or a stiff breeze. Following this there is the electronics part, which includes a wind sensor in addition to a simple quad photoresistor based light sensor. A couple of limit switches ensure that the system should never move past the point where worrying grinding and shearing noises begin. With assembly complete, the solar tracker is equipped with a single large panel and compared to a stationary identical panel and charge controller. This shows that the tracker nets one an additional 30-50% of energy in the two scenarios compared over the course of two days of testing. items.title: Where to See the World’s Most Famous Preserved Body Parts

Beyond the normal displays of skeletons in medical museums and holy leaders’ bodies in churches and temples, there’s a whole world of bits and pieces to explore. Throughout history, body parts have been taken as trophies during wartime, worshipped as miraculous healing agents, cut off and displayed to honor their owners, or simply saved incidentally by natural processes. items.title: “Men with Queer Nerves”: The Jumping Frenchmen of Maine
items.summary: In the late nineteenth century, visitors to Maine observed something strange: French-Canadian lumberjacks who, at the slightest stimulus, seemed to jump, strike out with their limbs, or mimic languages they could not speak. Ross Bullen introduces us to these so-called “Jumping Frenchmen” and to their greatest investigator, George M. Beard, who saw a link in their behavior between religious frenzy and neurasthenia.

items.title: Atlas Obscura’s Guide to America’s Most Haunted Cemeteries
items.summary: It’s nice to imagine death as an endless deep sleep, but not everyone is so lucky. In cemeteries across the U.S., you’ll find souls whose final resting places are not, in fact, restful at all. Perhaps they died with scores unsettled or, perhaps, their graves were ravaged by greedy developers. Sometimes, heartbreak rendered them unable to move on peacefully; in other cases, they simply couldn’t resist the chance to toy with their living visitors. One thing is certain: These restless spirits can turn otherwise serene sites into delightfully dark destinations, where the beauty of old headstones and manicured grounds is tinged with something indescribably eerie. items.summary: Nothing beats staying in a hotel whose suites hold some stories — especially if they’re of the spooky variety. Booking a room at a regular old hotel will give you a few nice photos and a comfy robe; booking a room at a haunted one will give you tales of terror to tell for the rest of your life. items.title: Philip Sidney and the Extreme (Dis)graces of the Parenthesis
items.summary: Erasmus called them “little moons” and George Puttenham praised them as “figures of tolerable disorder” (if used not too often “nor too thick”). For Philip Sidney, they were simply indispensable. Florence Hazrat introduces us to the uncontested early modern king of brackets and to his romance Arcadia , which abruptly ends, like its author’s life, hanging on a parenthesis.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
items.summary: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built specifically for robotics. To help developers put these capabilities to work, the new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity transforms the platform into a comprehensive workbench supporting rapid hardware bring-up, MuJoCo simulation, and closed-loop control. Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

items.title: Build full-stack Android apps with Gemini in Google AI Studio

items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide
items.summary: The newly launched AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide provides hardware-grounded design rules to help developers maximize performance on TPUs for LLMs and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workloads. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

items.title: Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch

items.title: Securing Your Agents: A Hands-On Guide to Agent Anomaly Detection
items.summary: This guide walks developers through setting up Agent Anomaly Detection on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to monitor AI agent telemetry and catch behavioral risks. It demonstrates how to deploy a sample customer support agent, trigger out-of-scope security findings, and configure proactive alerts using Cloud Monitoring and Security Command Center.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
items.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

It demonstrates how to catch prompt regressions, evaluate model backend swaps using side-by-side trace comparisons, and automate evaluation passes. Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

items.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

Switching from bundled binaries reduces app size by approximately 8 MB while enabling seamless, automatic runtime updates across billions of devices. Developers can easily adopt these updates by updating their dependencies and utilizing the new Android Studio LiteRT skill for automated migration.
